planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Radiance holds its coppery-pink new-frond color longer into the season than the species.

directions: New fronds emerge in a vivid mix of pink, orange, and red before maturing to glossy bright green by midsummer, then turning coppery again in fall for season-long color interest. The clump-forming, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen fronds reach 2 to 3 feet tall and wide, making it suitable for mass planting as a woodland understory groundcover or as a potted specimen. Plant in humus-rich soil with consistent moisture and divide congested clumps in spring if needed; established plants are notably deer and rabbit resistant.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil kept consistently moist, in partial to full shade; this slow-growing clumper resents root disturbance once established.

directions: A clonal fern selection collected in China by fern specialist Judith Jones of Fancy Fronds Nursery, closely related to Polystichum polyblepharum but with a distinctly glossy, plastic-like frond texture. New fronds unfurl with large coppery scales before settling into deep green, forming a tidy, upright, clumping evergreen rosette. It grows slowly and stays compact, making it well suited to shaded rock gardens or woodland edges where a refined, shiny-leaved texture is wanted. Keep soil evenly moist and avoid dry shade for best appearance.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this selection spreads slowly and is best left undisturbed once established.

directions: A selected form of the southeastern native wild ginger with glossy, heart-shaped, dark evergreen leaves overlaid with a dramatic, dense silver mottling pattern. Small, jug-shaped maroon-brown flowers hide beneath the foliage in spring, largely hidden from view at ground level. It forms a slowly spreading, tidy clump that works well as a textural accent along shaded path edges or in a woodland groundcover mix. Keep soil consistently moist and rich in organic matter; it resents hot, dry exposure.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this cultivar tolerates clay and periodically damp soil better than most Asarum and spreads faster by rhizomes.

directions: Large, leathery, arrowhead-shaped dark green leaves are heavily mottled with silver in a pattern reminiscent of a hardy cyclamen, making this one of the showiest-foliaged wild gingers in cultivation. Deep purple-brown, jug-shaped flowers are produced in spring but stay tucked beneath the foliage, mostly unseen. A rhizomatous spreader, it forms an evergreen groundcover clump at a faster rate than most Asian gingers and tolerates heavier, damp clay soils better than many relatives. Give it rich, evenly moist soil in shade for the fullest, most silvery leaf display.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; site where morning light can highlight the colorful emerging fronds without scorching them.

directions: A large, clump-forming selection of Wallich's wood fern discovered by Bob Hollister of Country Garden Plants in Dorset, England, whose new fronds unfurl in striking shades of golden orange before shifting through lime green and finally settling into dark green, each frond carried on a nearly black, scaly stipe for added contrast. The bold, upright, vase-shaped form stays tidy and evergreen to semi-evergreen through mild winters. It won a UK horticultural trade industry award recognizing it as a standout new ornamental plant introduction. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade for the best frond color and habit.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants 16-18 inches apart since this running groundcover fills in readily and can overrun closely spaced neighbors.

directions: Part of Chris Hansen's trademarked Feathered Friends series of bugleweeds, Fierce Falcon carries lustrous foliage so deeply dark purple it reads as nearly black year-round. Short, cobalt-blue flower spikes rise above the mat of leaves in mid to late spring for a brief but vivid color contrast. The ground-hugging, stoloniferous habit spreads steadily to form a dense evergreen mat, making it effective as a dramatic dark-leaved backdrop beneath shrubs or spring bulbs. Give it room to spread and divide congested patches every few years to keep it vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this miniature selection is still uncommon in the trade and increases slowly, so avoid crowding it with faster groundcovers.

directions: A dwarf selection of the native Allegheny spurge discovered and named at Ohio's Holden Arboretum, growing to only about one-half to one-third the size of the typical species. Its small, scalloped, dusty blue-green leaves form a low, slow-spreading clump that stays neatly in scale for small shaded gardens, rock garden pockets, or path edging where a full-size Allegheny spurge would be too large. Like the species, foliage often takes on mottled silver tones through winter before fresh growth emerges in spring. Still relatively rare in the nursery trade, it rewards patience with a tidy, long-lived groundcover clump.
